title: Morning at the Rajpoot House
body:
“Sameer, wake up — it’s late! You’ll miss the school bus,” someone hissed just outside my door.



My brain wanted five more minutes; my body wanted the same. The voice belonged to my mother. That was usually all it took. In our house, my mother’s voice had the authority of a thunderclap and the gentleness of a lullaby, often at the same time.



“Meet the commander of the house,” I mumbled into my pillow — Saima Khursheed Rajpoot — the woman who ran our home like a small, benevolent army. She had a way of waking the dead with a cup of tea and a schedule. This morning was no different.



Footsteps on the stairs. The smell of spice and frying eggs drifted under my door, and for a second I considered staying in bed forever just to hold onto that warmth.



“Leave him, Mama,” another voice called. “It’s already late. Make breakfast, please — and tell the girls and Nano to come. Don’t want to be late and be scolded by that ‘fat’ P.T. sir.”



I groaned and opened one eye. Mom’s exasperated chuckle came through the wood. “Beta, open your eyes. I have already made breakfast. Tell your sisters and Nano to come. Come on, mover and shaker.”



Nano — my grandmother — appeared to be hermit-level selective about mornings. She only left her room for weddings, big celebrations, or if someone had bribed her with perfectly sweet tea. Otherwise, she remained a mystery in her corner of the house, like an old queen on an unused throne.



From inside my doorway the noise grew louder. Saira and Sadia — twin hurricanes in matching clothes — were in their usual duet: competing over nothing and everything.



“Bhaiya, it’s been late! Wake up and get ready,” Saqib bellowed, voice already half a warning and half a demand. “Mom’s calling. If you’ve been possessed by that same jin Sameer has, then wake up, for God’s sake!” He delivered the last part with a weird, high-pitched laugh like a demon impersonation.



I pulled the blanket over my head and pretended to be possessed just so they’d stop. It rarely worked.



From the doorway I could see Saad standing halfway down the hall — tall, composed, with that look he reserved for small annoyances and people who politely refused to understand him. Saad was the oldest: graduated to high school, shoulders broader, jaw harder. He had a stare that could make small boys feel guilty for breathing too loudly.



Saqib, the second son, lounged on the stairs with his phone. Saqib gave a smile and a shrug — quieter than Saad but more dangerous in his silence. He had the sort of look that made you wonder whether he was listening or calculating. Today, he gave Saad a little grin and went back to scrolling. I could see the brothers’ small language — nothing but a look, and the house’s weather changed.



“Where are my tops?” Saira shrieked suddenly. “I just bought them yesterday. Who put them where? You hid them because I got the pink and you got the blue, didn’t you? Give them back, you—” Her language blurred into teenage fury: “burglar, thief, bitch.” The twins always used the same old repertoire; they had learned to rehearse fighting like a sport.



“Don’t have any manners girls,” Mom snapped, stepping between them like an umpire. “Have you prayed this morning? Huh Shame on you girls — the way you speak, what will people think?”



Sadia’s face went red. Saira turned furious, but Mom’s scolding was that single voice that could stop a war. For a moment they subsided into sullen silence and made their way to the dining table — both sulky, both impeccably dressed, both the same and entirely different.



My mother adjusted my father’s tie for him in the master bedroom as he stood by the mirror complaining about the time. Dad — Mr. Khurseheed Rajpoot — was the kind of man who carried an office in his posture: precise, a little old-fashioned, and used to having the last say at home and at work. Mom smoothed the creases in his shirt, kissed his cheek, and fussed over his bag like it was a child she trusted less than a kettle.



"Amma please! Tell Saira to give me her omelette! This witch ate hers already and now she’s doing brutality with mine.

Please Ammaaaa…” Sadia whined dramatically, holding an empty plate like a victim of world war.



Saira rolled her eyes, “Bhaiya, it’s always Sadia who picks a fight with me! I didn’t even say anything. But she still acts like I’m not her sister… worse than Sameer!”



The moment Sameer’s name slipped from her mouth—



Everyone always complained about Sameer — the stubborn, loud, reckless youngest child.

He annoyed the sisters, embarrassed Saqib, and even Nano rolled her eyes whenever he spoke.



But Saad?



Saad’s hatred was different.



More violent.

More personal.

More dangerous.



His fists clenched tight.



A nerve jumped near his temple.



His breathing sharpened like he was trying not to scream.



He stared at Saira like she had touched a wound no one was allowed to see.



“Don’t. Ever. Compare yourself to him,” he growled, voice low but trembling with something more than anger.

Something like fear.

Or guilt.



No one understood why Saad reacted like this…

Why the very mention of Sameer pushed him beyond reason.



But the reason?



It existed.



Buried deep.



And soon… everyone would know.



Saad didn’t stop there.



He turned sharply toward Sadia, as if she was the real target of his anger — not Saira.



“And you!” he snapped, voice slicing the air like a blade,

“Stop acting innocent for once! Every morning, every fight — you start it and then pretend you’re the victim!”



Sadia’s eyes widened — her lips trembling, breath stuck in her throat.

She had just asked for her omelette back… but this?

This was humiliation.

Cruel, unexpected, and loud.



“You think just because you’re older than me, you can misbehave and everyone will forgive you?”

Saad leaned forward, fury boiling over.

“You should be ashamed of how pathetic you act. Even Sameer has more dignity than you.”



That line broke her.



Her face went pale — like all the blood had rushed out of her body at once.

She held her breath to stop the tears threatening to escape…

But they betrayed her anyway.



She stood up abruptly, chair screeching across the floor, and ran toward her room — covering her mouth to hide her sobs.



Saira opened her mouth to defend her sister — but shock sealed her voice.



Sameer just stared at Saad… confused and afraid.



And that’s exactly when…



Footsteps echoed from the staircase.



Mr. Khursheed and Mrs. Saima appeared — both stunned at the chaos unfolding below.

Mr. Khursheed’s voice boomed:



“Beta Saad! Are you out of your mind?!”



Saad froze — the fire in his eyes instantly dimming into regret.



His father descended the last few steps with anger heavy in every step:



“Have you lost your senses — or have you made it your morning routine to create a circus here? Is she your slave? Or your enemy?!”



Saad tried to speak —

“Baba, I didn’t even—”



“DON’T lie!” his father roared,

“You think your age gives you the right to attack her like this? Even slaves are treated with more respect than what I just witnessed!”



Silence.



Everyone’s heads bowed low — except Saad…

He stood there, motionless, guilt burning through him.



Mr. Khursheed’s tone left no space for argument.



“Go upstairs. Right now.

Bring your sister back. She will finish breakfast with everyone.”



Saad pressed his teeth together.



His anger was still boiling —

but defying his father… that was another war.



“Yes, Baba,” he managed.



Saad nodded stiffly, anger still shaking inside him.



As he turned toward the corridor,

Saira’s glare followed him like a knife.



Not a normal sister fight glare —

but a warning.



A promise.



A silent:

“Touch her again like that… and you’ll regret it.”



Saira might fight Sadia every day,

but no one — no one — hurt her sister except her.



Saad saw that stare.



His jaw tightened.



But when his eyes lowered and accidentally met Sameer’s…



That was different.



His stare toward Sameer was pure poison.



A burning message: “All of this is because of YOU.”



Sameer looked down instantly —

chest tight, breath weak.



He wasn’t scared of his sisters.

He wasn’t scared of Nano.



He wasn’t even scared of Baba.



But Saad’s hatred?



That was a storm he had been surviving for years.

Everyone fell silent.



Saira stared at her plate, regretting the moment she dragged Sameer’s name into this.



Nano muttered something under her breath: “Roz ka drama…”



Sameer just glanced down, pretending he wasn’t the storm’s center.



Saad took a deep breath and knocked — once.

No answer.



He knocked harder.



“Sadia… open the door,” he said through his teeth.



Still quiet.



He almost walked away — almost —

but Baba’s voice echoed sharp in his head.



So he spoke again, this time with a fake softness:



“Api… please. Come back. Baba wants you at the table.”



Inside, Sadia wiped her tears fast.



She wasn’t crying because she was weak —

but because Saad’s hatred always cut the deepest.



She opened the door just a little, eyes red but her chin high.



Saad avoided eye contact —

his apology was a script, not a feeling.



“Sorry,” he said, monotone.

“We shouldn’t fight… especially not in front of everyone.

Now come downstairs.”



No warmth.

No guilt.

Just orders wrapped as apologies.



Sadia stared at him for a second…

then nodded silently.



Not for him.

For Baba.



“Baba, can I have fifty rupees more?” I heard myself ask before I could stop it. “We have a class party — the ma’am said everyone has to bring fifty rupees.”



Dad reached into his wallet with a half-annoyed, half-amused look. “Yes of course, my brave son. Take this one hundred and enjoy,” he said, easily handing me a small roll of notes like he always did. “Tell me about the party tonight, and don’t come back late.”



I slipped the money into my pocket and smiled at him. He smiled back with that mixture of pride and the want to be more authoritative than he felt. It was a well-practiced dance at our table.



The twins sulked but obeyed. Nano shuffled in at last, her movements slow but ceremonious, wrapped in a shawl. She sat down like a queen arriving at court and glanced around with a small, sharp glance that could cut through pretense. She didn’t speak much, but when she did, everyone paid attention because it almost always made sense.



Saad came back to the table and sat down beside me. He looked pale, restless. He had been my brother since I could remember, but lately there had been a distance — not all of it his fault. Sometimes older brothers carry storms that land on smaller ones.



After breakfast, the house moved into its usual choreography. Saira and Sadia gathered their books and argued in whispers over lipstick. Nano waved one hand as if swatting away the noise, then settled into a chair by the window with a small cup of sweet tea. Dad double-checked his briefcase, kissed Mom on the cheek in a small ritual of two people who had been running the same path for years, and Saad grabbed his backpack, ran a hand through his hair, and left for the school bus.



Saqib lingered at the door for a moment and then headed out, the sort of brother who smiled at small cruelties with an almost friendly tilt. He had watched Sadia’s face when Saad apologized; he had that smaller-brother amusement you get when the world is still solving its problems in slow motion. He grinned and gave me the look that said, See you at home, man, and I’ll tease you about it later.



As the van pulled away, I felt the house flatten a little — like the sun had been covered by a cloud. I thought about the bruise forming behind my ear and the sticky taste of blood on my lip that I’d hidden from everyone. I thought about Aareen’s frightened face and her hands pressing on my chest in the canteen, the way everything had gone silent except for the sirens and the steady march of time.



Mom noticed my quiet. “You okay, beta?” she asked, with that soft worry reserved for small tragedies.



“Fine, Ma,” I said. “Just tired.”



She studied me for a beat longer and then nodded. “Eat properly and don’t keep things to yourself. You know where to get me.”



I stood, pocketed the extra money, and kissed her cheek. She smelled like cinnamon and something that always made me feel like home.



At the front gate, Saad paused and turned back once more. Our eyes met and he mouthed, Be careful. I returned a small affirmative nod. He got on the bus and took his seat near the window, looking out over the road as if he were surveying his kingdom.



The van pulled away, and the house settled into its daytime hush — except for the small storm still simmering in the corners: Sadia’s hurt, Saad’s impatience, Saqib’s quiet smile, and my own bruises. Nano’s chair creaked as she adjusted herself, and Mom took to her kitchen tasks as if by stirring a pot she could rearrange the weather.



I wondered, as the bus disappeared into the distance, whether a morning could carry so much weight. The apologies that shook nothing, the money for a party, a mother’s kiss, a sister’s tears — it all felt like threads pulled from the same fabric. Pull one wrong way and something would unravel.



I shoved my hands into my pockets and headed toward the school gate. Outside, the world moved with its small, greedy appetite. Inside, a quiet thing in me tightened: the part that didn’t want anyone else to see the bruise under my hair, the part that didn’t want to be a bother. I walked, as always, trying to be smaller than I felt and stronger than I looked.



And somewhere, between blink and breath, the day began.
